posts.title: Five words for harbour fog
posts.excerpt: A ship’s log, one morning of fog and a glossary entry that took a week.
posts.content:
A harbour museum asked us to translate an old ship’s log into five languages. On the third page the captain writes about a fog that sits low on the water and lifts by noon, and he uses a word only sailors on this coast still know.

We asked two retired pilots at the ferry landing. In the end each language got its own coastal word rather than a plain “fog”, and the glossary entry now has a short note on where every one of them comes from.

posts.title: Why we still open paper dictionaries
posts.excerpt: The word next to the one you wanted is often the one you need.
posts.content:
Our shelf holds forty years of dictionaries, some older than the studio. We use the screen too, of course, but every translator here starts with a book open on the desk.

A page shows you the neighbours of a word, its older meanings and the example a careful editor chose fifty years ago. That is often where the right sentence is hiding.

posts.title: Translating a picture book, one page turn at a time
posts.excerpt: In a picture book the joke has to land when the page turns, in every language.
posts.content:
This autumn we finished a picture book about a cat who rides the ferry every morning. The text is only three hundred words, and it took longer than a contract ten times its length.

Every sentence has to fit the picture beside it and leave the surprise for the next page. We read each version aloud to a child in that language before we sent it to the publisher.
